A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TrajICL research. All 16 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices, support comparison. Reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original trajectory-prediction experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations, and qualitative results, including ETH-UCY evaluation in its appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds sports-domain evaluation, robustness experiments, architecture studies, and computational measurements.

M1.justification: v2 adds experimental architectural and inference variants: ForecastMAE with its lane encoder disabled and repeated application of PG-ES (Tables 8 and 17). The standard STES/PG-ES procedure, RCPE/SRPE components, loss, and two-stage training remain unchanged. Renaming PredictionHead to MultiModalDecoder is cosmetic.

E1.justification: v2 adds NBA SportVU rebounding and scoring subsets, extending evaluation into basketball motion. It also introduces detector/tracker-generated JRDB inputs and short-observation scenarios. ETH-UCY was already evaluated in v1's appendix and is retained, not newly added.

E2.justification: Tables 8 and 11–12 add ForecastMAE comparisons, reported RAN/MetaTra comparisons, and prompt-selection comparisons including feature similarity. RAN/MetaTra use differing architectures and training settings, so their scores do not establish matched-setting superiority. The original fine-tuning comparator set remains; identifying VPT Shallow with the Latent Corridors approach clarifies an existing comparator.

E3.justification: Added evaluation designs vary model dimensions (32/64/128), predictor depth (1/2/3), PG-ES iterations (1–4), and observation length (9/6/3 timesteps). v2 also introduces computational profiling and feature-distribution FID evaluation. The original chronological 80/20 split, K=20 prediction metrics, and 100-plus-400-epoch training schedule remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analysis with architecture/backbone studies, alternative selectors, perception-error and short-history robustness, iterative refinement, initial-error analysis, pool-quality analysis, and synthetic-to-real feature comparisons. Existing VTP, RCPE/SRPE, and pool-size studies remain. Figure 6 replaces v1's WildTrack pool-size comparison with an example-count comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new scatterplots show variation across samples rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 and the ETH-UCY results remain numerically unchanged. v2 adds architecture, basketball, robustness, cost, and diagnostic results; for example, Table 15 reports noisy-input JRDB minFDE20 of 4.33 for Social-Transmotion versus 2.79 for TrajICL. Figures 3 and 6 also contain revised curves without a corresponding explanation of changed experimental settings.

T1.justification: The retrieval equations, training objective, and substantive mathematical formulation are retained. Section 3.1 explicitly describes K possible futures, restating the multimodal output already present in v1's Equation 5. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims remain adaptation without parameter updates, STES and PG-ES example selection, and synthetic training enabling cross-domain prediction. Merging the synthetic-data contribution into the first contribution and removing some uses of 'rapid' do not substantively redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes reduced adaptation cost from increased inference cost and documents failure with a small NBA example pool. It adds explanations linking PG-ES benefits to ambiguous initial predictions, pool relevance, and synthetic-to-real transfer. Appendix A.3 also explicitly qualifies comparisons across different architectures and training datasets.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies eight context examples, dataset sampling rates and corresponding time horizons, precomputed context features, profiling hardware, batch-one memory measurement, and the upstream detector/tracker models. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original experiments. The project-page link is effectively unchanged, and the PDFs do not establish changed code availability.

R1.justification: Section 2's positioning is largely retained. New appendix discussion addresses architecture-coupled adaptation methods and comparison fairness, while additional citations support prompt-selection strategies, basketball evaluation, perception models, and efficiency discussion. Reference deduplication and bibliographic corrections do not remove substantive prior work.

P1.justification: The main narrative receives local wording corrections, expanded adaptation explanations, a merged contribution list, and terminology changes. The appendix is reorganized from one broad experimental subsection into A.1–A.6. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds architecture, sports, robustness, and cost tables plus initial-error and pool-similarity scatterplots, and substantially rearranges appendix displays. Several example-count plots are redrawn. The old qualitative Figure 9 becomes Figure 11. Figure 6 replaces mismatched panels, but Figure 7 introduces duplicated JTA plots under the MOTSynth label.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses important gaps in v1's practical validation: Tables 13–14 quantify adaptation savings and inference overhead, while Tables 15–16 test perception errors and limited observations. Backbone evaluation and the explicitly reported small-pool failure further clarify applicability. Figure 7's mislabeled duplication and the continued absence of uncertainty reporting limit confidence in parts of the evidence, but the added tests and qualifications materially strengthen support for the paper's central deployment claims.
